issues.description: Regex HAS_TIME conflates 'a digit followed by ms or s' with 'a time value'
issues.detail: The guard /\dm?s/i answers 'might this string contain a time value?' but it's not the same predicate as 'this declaration has a time the rule cares about'. It will match things like '12s' inside a url() or string, '3ms' in a custom property, or '4s' in a content: literal. That's fine as a fast pre-filter (false positives just fall through to the existing parser), but the name HAS_TIME overstates what the regex actually decides. Naming it something like LIKELY_HAS_TIME or PREFILTER_TIME would keep the value (a cheap rejection) separate from the identity (the authoritative check, which is still valueParser). Right now the name complects 'cheap heuristic' with 'truth about time-ness'.

issues.description: The optimization is a guard, not a decomposition; the underlying walkDecls body still does the real work
issues.detail: This patch is a fine local speedup: skip the expensive parse on declarations that obviously have no time token. But the rule body still complects 'is this declaration in scope' (property name, ignore list, delay handling) with 'parse the value' with 'walk parsed nodes and report'. The hot path here was dominated by parsing every declaration's value, including values with no time at all; the real simplification is that the rule was asking valueParser a question it could have answered from the raw string. A cleaner shape pushes the 'does this value mention a time' check and the 'is this property in scope' check to the edge, and only then parses. The PR does the first half of that; worth noting the second half (property-name filter before parse) is also still available and would compose with this change.

issues.description: Property-name lookup moved after the regex guard but could move earlier for additional rejection
issues.detail: decl.prop.toLowerCase() + vendor.unprefixed() is now only paid when HAS_TIME matches, which is good. But propertyName is still computed for every time-bearing declaration even when the rule will not act on that property at all. The set of properties the rule actually cares about is knowable; a property-name filter would be a second cheap rejection before any parsing. Not required for this PR, just naming the next move so the change doesn't look like the optimization is finished.

review.summary: SIMPLE-ENOUGH for the scope of the patch. The change is a cheap pre-filter regex that skips the expensive valueParser call when the declaration value clearly contains no time token; this is a legitimate guard at the edge of the hot loop and the kind of decomposition that respects the actual cost model. The remaining concerns are naming (HAS_TIME overstates what the regex decides; it's a heuristic, not the authoritative predicate) and that the larger complecting in the rule body (scope check, parse, walk, report all intermingled) is untouched — this patch is a local speedup, not a redesign, and that's a reasonable choice for a bug-fix PR. No correctness risk: the regex is a superset of real time values, so anything it lets through still hits the existing logic. Ship.
